claims.text: A critical level of configurational entropy creates a locally disordered, electronically optimized environment in a BCC high-entropy alloy.
High configurational entropy enhances BCS-type superconductivity by balancing increased electron–phonon coupling against disorder-induced scattering.
Reducing alloy complexity while holding average electron count, lattice parameters, and phase purity constant lowers effective electron–phonon coupling.
Reduced alloy complexity suppresses or lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti can form a BCC high-entropy alloy with randomly distributed constituent elements.
The proposed as-cast Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti starting material is single-phase and maximally disordered.
Matching average electron count, lattice constant, BCC structure, phase purity, and processing between the series isolates configurational entropy as the changed variable.
High configurational entropy drives atomic-scale compositional disorder.
Atomic-scale disorder modulates the local electronic density of states and phonon spectra.
Localized lattice distortions caused by disorder enhance electron–phonon coupling in the dirty limit.
Superconducting (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x is consistent with single-band isotropic s-wave superconductivity in the dirty limit.
Reducing configurational entropy produces a less heterogeneous distribution of local lattice distortions and thereby diminishes electron–phonon coupling efficiency.
The full-complexity Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti alloy should exhibit a superconducting transition below 10 K.
Entropy-reduced variants should have a suppressed or shifted transition temperature relative to the full-complexity alloy.
Entropy-reduced variants should have increased residual resistivity and lower critical magnetic fields.
The proposed entropy-dependent trend should hold only while BCC structure, average electron count, lattice constant, and phase purity remain unchanged.

contradictions.description: The mediator states that greater high-entropy disorder increases scattering, but the prediction assigns increased residual resistivity to the entropy-reduced, nominally less-disordered variants.

The control is described as fully disordered and as-cast, whereas the conditions require annealing for stress relief across both sample sets; it is unclear whether the actual baseline remains as-cast.

The boundary and uncertainty fields say that unintended electron-count or structural changes invalidate or confound the comparison, but the falsification rule treats correlation with those unintended changes as evidence refuting the entropy mechanism.
